newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr finds good and bad in Fed inaction.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr finds good and bad in Fed inaction.

text.p: The Australian dollar ground to a softer finish Wednesday as aggressive U.S. selling offshore was only partly mopped up by stubborn Asian demand.

The currency did derive some support from the Federal Reserve's decision not to hike U.S. rates. However, while that safeguarded the dollar's yield premium for the moment, it may have actually increased the risk of a domestic rate cut.
An anxiously awaited speech by Australia's new Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane turned out to be an excitement-free affair more tuned to his economist audience than the markets.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar had struggled back to US$0.7880/85 after delving as deep as US$0.7852 offshore, but was still short of Tuesday's late US$0.7893/98.
Traders said U.S. fund selling had been quite heavy overnight -- a single player dumped around A$300 million in one go -- so the resilience of US$0.7855 support had surprised.
Some of the demand was linked to a strangle options play and there were also rumours of a A$250 million dual currency samurai issue, but no actual evidence and dealers were sceptical.
On the crosses, the currency bounced to 86.40/50 yen from an early 85.97/07 and was almost back to Tuesday's late 86.54/64.
In trade weighted terms it remained softer at 58.0 from a previous 58.2 close.

The U.S. dollar was an influence in both directions as it first slid in disappointment at the Fed's inaction, only to recoup much of its losses on heavy Japanese importer and fund buying. In both cases the local currency followed it slavishly.
The Fed's decision had conflicting implications in other ways. In the very near term it was a relief to A$ bulls since a hike would have trimmed the currency's interest rate advantage.
However, bears argued the lack of a U.S. hike actually made a cut here more likely.
"It has removed one potential risk for the AUD, so in that sense the RBA could be more comfortable about easing," said Anthony Thompson, an economist at Hongkong Bank Australia.
"For the AUD it was almost a case of damned if you do, damned if you don't," he said about the Fed's choice on rates.

Furthermore, many analysts still expected the Fed to tighten by at least 0.25 point before year-end, probably at its next meeting on November 13, while predicting a 0.5 point easing in domestic rates at the RBA's board meeting on November 5.
That scenario was a nightmare for dollar bulls which was why the market was hanging on every word from Macfarlane today.

In the event, he confined himself to a defence of the banks' independence record and a general comment that the endorsement by the government of its inflation target would help improve the country's medium term economic performance.

Domestic economic data is thin on the ground this week but a survey on business expectations for the fourth quarter offered a reasonably upbeat outlook. Firms expected profits to rise 3.7 percent in Q4 and sales to rise 1.6 percent.
Capital spending was seen up 2.6 percent compared to a 2.0 percent rise in the September quarter. However, firms also expected selling prices to rise a very modest 0.2 percent.

The Westpac-Melbourne Institute leading index of economic activity showed a similar mix of firmer growth and subdued inflation. The July index rose by 2.5 points or 1.7 percent taking annual growth to 3.4 percent from 0.1 percent in June.
But the leading index of inflation fell again by 0.2 percentage points to 4.5 percent from 4.7 percent in June.

Westpac's general manager, economics, Bill Evans said the strong rise in the leading index promised an upturn in growth from mid-1997, but that did not preclude another easing in policy given the subdued inflation outlook.
-- Wayne Cole 61-2 373 1800
